chapter_theme: The last songs at Swamimalai (சுவாமி மலை, also called Eragam): the poet confesses the diseases of a sinful life, his spending on women's jewels, and courtesans who dance in the street, drug a man and take his gold, and in the last song his refusal to share with the hungry before Death comes; the praise returns to Murugan as teacher of Siva and Brahma's humbler, and to the Rama story.
structure_note: All eight follow the two halves. 234 to 238 are confessions of women and courtesans; 232 is a catalogue of diseases, 233 of spending on women, 239 of hoarding before death. Five songs name the shrine Eragam (ஏரகம்) or the Mantra-guru hill rather than Swamimalai.

232.reading: The poet lists the diseases that have come on him, wind, colic, scrofula, swellings, cough, ringworm and the sores he calls the ornaments women give, which keep him to his bed; through them he has forgotten the love of Murugan's flower feet and drunk sin like liquor. Caught in the net of bonds in a low birth, he asks Murugan to come with grace and rule him before he is ruined and called a fool. The praise is only of Swamimalai, its groves of mango and konrai, its walls reaching the clouds and its flags.
232.nuance: மாதர்தரு பூஷணங்கள், 'ornaments women give', is bitter irony: the diseases caught from women are the jewels they return for the jewels given them. பாதகவியாதி, 'diseases of sin', ties illness to fault. The word in line 12 is corrupt and its sense uncertain.

233.reading: The poet tells how he grew old in friendship with women, wandering from youth after kohl-eyed girls and seeking wealth to buy them gold ornaments, earrings and pearls, and asks whether he must go on wandering in such pain of spirit. The praise names the hero who drove off Sura and split him to the root, the nephew of the charioteer Vishnu, and Eragam among high paddy fields where farmers raise water.
233.nuance: The confession is of spending: பொருள்தேடி, 'seeking wealth', for women's ornaments (மாபணிக்கள், ஓலை, முத்தம்). The epithet சூகரத்தொடு அம்பு தானெடுத்து வந்த சூதன் may join Vishnu's boar form to the charioteer Krishna; the reading of the opening lines and of this epithet is uncertain.

234.reading: The poet describes at length the beauty of dancing women like Rambha, from their hair, earrings, teeth and lips to their breasts, waist and thighs, who sing in cuckoo voices and twist, smile and dance in the street, and asks whether it is fit to keep company with these deceivers who serve Kama's bed. The praise is a battle in which the sea roars, jackals and vultures feed, the mountain is struck and the elephants of the directions shake as Murugan sends the vel with a smile; he weds Indra's daughter and the hunter girl and stands at Eragam.
234.nuance: The whole charge sits in the last line of the confession: குத்திரர், deceivers, and சந்தமாமோ, 'is it fitting?'. Dancing in the street (நற்றெருமீதில் ... நடிப்பவர்) suggests temple or street dancers, but no payment is named. The final epithet, லக்ஷுமி பெற்றருள், is unclear to me.

235.reading: The poet describes courtesans who loosen and toss their hair, roll their spear eyes, laugh 'come', show their bodies like puppets on strings, slip their garments, dance and sing like cuckoos, draw a man close, dose him with a drug and strip him of his wealth, and asks whether a bond with these false dancers is right. The praise names the vel that burned Sura's hill, the father who kicked Death, Uma as mother, and the hunter girl, at Eragam.
235.nuance: மருத்திட்டு ஆட்டி, 'dosing him with medicine', and சீர்பொருள் பறி, 'snatching his wealth', make these women thieves as well as lures; பொய்க் கூத்தர், false dancers, joins the two. The lines on Siva who kicked Death (கூற்றை மாளிட உதைத்து) and wears a skin may say that Murugan taught him (எனப்பர்க்கு ஏற்றி), but the syntax is not clear to me.

236.reading: The poet describes women's eyes, like poison, the vel and Kama's arrows, their musk-scented breasts like the northern mountain, their anklets, flowered hair, moon faces and swan gait, and asks whether he may melt and waste in union with them. The praise tells the whole Rama story, the golden deer, Kara, the seven sala trees, Vali's chest, the demon army and the ten crowned heads of Lanka's king, and names Murugan as that Rama's nephew, who mounted the peacock and circled the world in an instant, at Swamimalai.
236.nuance: The plea is one question, கலவியில் நைந்துருகிடலாமோ, 'may I melt in union?', after nine lines of description. உலகை வலமாக நொடியினில் வந்து, circling the world in a moment, recalls the story of the fruit contest, but the text gives only the circling.

237.reading: The poet describes the hair, carp eyes, earrings, brow, smile and breasts of courtesans who dance in anklets, and asks whether his drowning in infatuation with these deceivers and enchantresses will never end. The praise names Siva who wears the flayed elephant and tiger skin and shares his body with Uma, and Murugan as the guru Siva bows to; the vel that broke the seven seas; Vishnu as uncle; and Murugan who came to the millet field as an old man and beguiled the hunter girl, at the Mantra-guru hill.
237.nuance: கணிகையர் சழக்கர் விஞ்சையர் piles three names on the women: courtesans, deceivers, sorceresses. அவர்பணி குருபர, 'the guru whom he serves', puts Siva at Murugan's feet. மந்திர குருமலை, the hill of the mantra-guru, names Swamimalai by that teaching.

238.reading: The poet tells how women bewitch with their eyes, slip their breast-cloths and drown a man in the fire of lust, agree to deceitful play once red gold is spread before them as the price, and after a few days quarrel with unheard-of words, and asks for Murugan's ever-fresh feet with golden anklets and vetchi flowers. The praise names Siva who raised his foot against Yama, Murugan's marriages, and the Murugan who once told the truth so that the old Veda-knower Brahma was ashamed, at Eragam.
238.nuance: விலையாக மிக்க செம்பொன், gold 'as the price', and the quarrel that follows (சிலுகாகி) are the courtesan story in brief, and the bond is called முழுமாயை, wholly illusion. முதுவேதன் வெட்க ... திருவாய்மை செப்பி is the story of Brahma's ignorance, here without naming Om. The epithets for the two consorts (புருகூதன், ம்ருகக் கரும்பு) are uncertain to me.

239.reading: The poet asks whether he must fail and perish, having refused to share food with the hungry who came to him, kept his wealth for his hands and his youth, strayed from grace and suffered in pride, and taken this body to be lasting until kin surround it weeping, drums beat and Death takes the life. The praise names Murugan as the one who spoke agreeably to Siva, who gave half his body to Uma, who fed his foes to vultures, and who seeks out those who leave the quarrels of religions for austerity; the song ends at Thani.
239.nuance: The confession is of not giving: பசியுற்றவருக்கு அமுதைப் பகிர்தற்கு இசையாதே, refusing to share food with the hungry, set against the funeral (தமர் சுற்றி யழப் பறைகொட்டியிட). சமயச் சிலுகிட்டவரைத் தவறி, leaving those who quarrel over religions, is unusual praise: Murugan seeks those who go beyond sect.

links.note: The Kural says one who neither gives nor enjoys has nothing however rich; 239 is the confession of such a man, who kept his wealth for his hands and youth and shared nothing with the hungry, and finds it at the funeral.
Both set sharing food against the funeral drum and the wailing kin: 23 resolves to share even a grain before the summons, 239 confesses that he never did.

source_issues: Song 232: one corrupt character in வெற஧முடி (line 12); the intended word is unclear to me.
Song 234: one corrupt character in துண்டக்஡ணவ (line 3); ஡ண probably stands for ரீ (க்ரீவ, neck), as in song 12. Also unflagged சங்மாக (line 15), probably சங்கமாக.
Song 239: filed under சுவாமி மலை but ends at தணியிற் குமரப் பெருமாளே, which appears to name Thiruthani; the heading may be wrong, or தணி may be read otherwise.
